I am 58 years old and have farmed these fields for 40 years. With only my wife and me working the land—our son has a factory job in the city—I need a plan that fits two pairs of hands but still brings in enough cash. I have 7.5 mu total, and I know the wheat-maize double crop is the backbone of our food security and income stability. The well gives me reliable water, so I am not at the mercy of the rain as much as some neighbors.

This year, I will keep 6 mu in the wheat-maize rotation. In autumn, I will sow improved wheat seed after rotary tillage. I trust the old varieties like Jimai or Luyuan series; they have done well on my land for years. I will apply compound fertilizer as a basal dose and top-dress urea at green-up and jointing. With well irrigation, I will irrigate four times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, then at jointing, heading, and grain filling. I expect about 1,050 jin per mu if the spring weather cooperates. I will spray a pre-emergence herbicide, watch for aphids and scab, and probably need four pesticide applications in total. After harvesting wheat in early June, I will immediately plant Denghai hybrid maize without tillage—there is no time to waste between crops, and direct seeding after wheat stubble works better every year. I will side-dress nitrogen at the big-flare stage and irrigate twice in summer, at jointing and tasseling, unless the rains are generous. Corn borer is the main threat, so three pesticide sprays should cover it. Yield should be around 1,100 jin per mu.

On the remaining 1.5 mu, I will plant kohlrabi in spring. It is more work, but the county market pays well for it, and my wife can handle the harvest. I will rotary-till that plot to a fine seedbed and use improved kohlrabi seed. Kohlrabi needs plenty of potassium for the bulbs to swell, so I will push the potash higher than on my grain crops. I will irrigate three times and stay on top of cabbage worms and soft rot—likely five pesticide applications. I expect about 2,500 kg per mu from that plot. This mix keeps us fed, covers our expenses, and does not demand more labor than two old farmers can manage.
